A known diet: what keeping unidentified prey changes

Source: vignettes/known-diet.Rmd
known-diet.Rmd

In a real survey you never know what a predator actually ate; you only know what could still be identified. This vignette uses an invented survey in which the true diet is known. Two predators, 150 stomachs each, eat six prey species with fixed probabilities. Identification is then degraded with digestion, faster for copepods than for malacostracans (shrimps, crabs, amphipods) and faster for malacostracans than for fish. The script that builds the table is data-raw/simulate_known_diet.R in the package’s source repository.

library(DietView)
f   <- function(x) system.file("extdata", x, package = "DietView")
sim <- read.csv(f("dietview_sim.csv"), na.strings = c("NA", ""))
lin <- read.csv(f("dietview_sim_lineage.csv"), na.strings = c("NA", ""))
spec <- dv_spec(predator = "predator_species_common_name", stomach = "stomach_id",
                prey_name = "verified_name", weight = "prey_weight",
                digestion = "digestion_level_id", covariates = c("period", "region"))
prep <- dv_prepare(sim, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lin, verbose = FALSE)
prep
#> <dietview_prep>
#>   records   : 686 
#>   stomachs  : 300 
#>   predators : 2 
#>   ranks     : kingdom > phylum > class > order > family > genus > species 
#>   covariates: period, region 
#>   source    : table

Three versions of the same diet

For all records pooled, we compare the class composition, by records, in three ways:

  • truth: the class of the species each record really was;
  • kept: what DietView reports, with an unidentified share;
  • dropped: the common practice of removing unidentified records and rescaling the rest to 100%.
tree <- dv_build_tree(prep$data, prep$ranks, weight_col = "prey_weight")
obs  <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Class")

full_lin   <- read.csv(f("dietview_example_lineage.csv"), na.strings = c("NA", ""))
true_class <- full_lin$class[match(prep$data$true_species, full_lin$verified_name)]
truth      <- 100 * prop.table(table(true_class))

ident <- obs[obs$label != "NA", ]
cmp <- data.frame(class = names(truth), truth = round(as.numeric(truth), 1))
cmp$kept    <- round(ident$pct_occ[match(cmp$class, ident$label)], 1)
cmp$dropped <- round(100 * ident$pct_occ[match(cmp$class, ident$label)] / sum(ident$pct_occ), 1)
cmp <- rbind(cmp, data.frame(class = "unidentified at class", truth = 0,
                             kept = round(sum(obs$pct_occ[obs$label == "NA"]), 1),
                             dropped = NA))
cmp
#>                   class truth kept dropped
#> 1              Copepoda  21.9 17.1    18.6
#> 2          Malacostraca  48.7 45.8    49.9
#> 3             Teleostei  29.4 28.9    31.5
#> 4 unidentified at class   0.0  8.3      NA

Three things are worth seeing in this table.

  1. Neither version recovers the truth. Keeping unidentified records does not put them back where they belong. It leaves 8.3% of the records in a category of its own.
  2. Dropping them shifts the proportions toward prey that keep their identity. In this simulation copepods were set to lose their identity faster than fish, so it is no surprise that they are under-represented once unidentified records are removed: the direction is an input, not a finding. What the table shows is how the rescaled percentages look: complete and precise, with nothing to tell the reader that a correction was made.
  3. Keeping them tells you how big the problem could be. When records are lost but never misidentified, which is the case here, a class’s true share lies between its kept share and its kept share plus the unidentified share. That bound is arithmetic, not a result of the simulation, and it holds for any survey with the same property. The simulation only makes it visible. Dropping the unidentified records removes the bound along with them.

Where the identification was lost

Only in a simulation can we ask which prey ended up unidentified:

round(100 * tapply(is.na(prep$data$class), true_class, mean), 1)
#>     Copepoda Malacostraca    Teleostei 
#>           22            6            2

This is the share of records, for each true class, that could not be named at class. In real data the same pattern shows up indirectly, through dv_digestion_diagnostic(). The digestion profile and the unidentified share are what a reader needs to judge a fine-rank result. On the ICES extract that ships with the package (?ices_diet) there is no true_species column to compare with: the unidentified share by rank and the digestion profile, shown for those data in the getting-started and digestion vignettes, are all a real survey gives you.

What this does and does not show

The simulation is built so that identification loss depends on digestion and prey class, which is what the diet literature reports (Baker et al. 2014; Buckland et al. 2017). The direction of the bias is therefore an assumption, and its size depends on made-up parameters. Neither is a result, and neither should be quoted. What the vignette demonstrates is a mechanism: rescaling to the identified fraction hides whatever bias identification loss introduced, while keeping the unidentified share shows how large it could be.

To get a size that means something for your own survey, replace the identification-loss model in data-raw/simulate_known_diet.R with rates estimated from real data. Among records identified at least to class, the class is known, so a logistic regression of “identified to species” on digestion score and class gives class-specific loss rates below class. Loss above class cannot be observed directly; state the assumption you make about it. The size of the shift is then an estimate conditional on that stated assumption, and can be reported as such.

References

Baker, R., Buckland, A., & Sheaves, M. (2014). Fish gut content analysis: robust measures of diet composition. Fish and Fisheries, 15, 170–177.

Buckland, A., Baker, R., Loneragan, N., & Sheaves, M. (2017). Standardising fish stomach content analysis: the importance of prey condition. Fisheries Research, 196, 126–140.
